subject: How to resolve an issue using the FIML function?

messages.author: dee87689031662c2
messages.subject: How to resolve an issue using the FIML function?
parts:
I am currently analyzing my data for my thesis research, and an issue has come up that we do not know how to resolve. I have two time points, and I am conducting various path analyses in R with lavaan installed.

 

The issue I am having is with accounting for missing data. Since this is a longitudinal study, only 66% of participants completed both time points. I know that the default estimator with the lavaan package is maximum likelihood. However, this estimator removes cases that did not complete both time points from my analyses. Therefore, I resorted to use full information maximum likelihood estimator. However, when I use the function (missing = “ML”), my results come out strange. For instance, my r-square results are abnormally high, and my parameter estimates become very different from the default estimator and are very large as well. We think something isn’t right with my missing data function.

 

Does anyone know what might be causing this issue? Is there a better way to account for missing data in my longitudinal design with the lavaan package in R?

 

Your help and advice is greatly appreciated, as I feel like I am hitting a wall right now.  Thank you!

messages.author: 9b7a59c6f2d552cc
messages.subject: Re: How to resolve an issue using the FIML function?
parts:
Hi Jessica

The problem with FIML and any other imputation method (In My Opinion) is that they maximise the start values (M, SD, covariance & correlation matrices) of the known values before fitting the model. This inflates the model to correspond to the full data.

Recommended limits on imputation are 5% missing from Little & Rubin, whereas I’ve made a career habit of allowing 10% missing. After that we have no way of knowing if the missing is psychologically true when imputed. Even though the algorithm will work with very high % of missing data. It just doesn't mean it's true.

My strategy is always to conduct MVA outside SEM (I use EM) and decide which participants to keep and impute by inspecting the impact of MVA before analysis.

I think the problem you have identified is because you are imputing too much missing without checking that it is valid.

In repeated measures the best you can hope for is to save people who missed only a little data and accept that your working dataset will be much smaller than 100%

 

Little, R. J. A., & Rubin, D. B. (2002). Statistical analysis with missing data (2nd ed.). Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons.
